strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: voxel-level interpretability of brain encoding models, extending beyond prior group-level or coarse approaches.

The proposed method (LaVCa) is a reasonably clean modular pipeline (encoding model -> optimal image retrieval -> MLLM captioning -> LLM keyword extraction -> sentence composition) that decouples image captioning from sentence generation, allowing flexible substitution of vision/LLM components without specialized fine-tuning—an advantage over the end-to-end BrainSCUBA baseline.

Extensive quantitative evaluation across four NSD subjects, multiple voxel subsets (top 1k/3k/5k/10k), sentence-level and image-level prediction metrics, plus a shuffle control that validates the evaluation metric is sensitive to caption-voxel correspondence.

Good ablation studies (Appendix A.3) examining the effect of number of optimal images, number of extracted keywords, and choice of keyword-extraction model (gpt-4o vs Llama vs TextGraphParser), which supports the design choices.

Interesting qualitative/exploratory analyses (UMAP embeddings, word clouds, ROI shuffling) revealing fine-grained functional heterogeneity within classically defined ROIs (e.g., OFA, PPA), which is a potentially valuable neuroscientific contribution beyond just methodology.
Reasonable effort toward fair comparison with BrainSCUBA despite the original code being unavailable (temperature sweep, same image dataset, same encoding model training procedure).
weaknesses: BrainSCUBA baseline is a self-reimplementation (not the original codebase/checkpoints), and several components differ from the original paper (image dataset restricted to OpenImages only, training procedure for encoding weights via ridge regression instead of gradient descent, undisclosed image subset in original). This introduces significant uncertainty as to whether the reported improvement over BrainSCUBA is due to LaVCa's core contribution or to reimplementation artifacts/undertuning of the baseline.

The evaluation metrics (sentence-level and image-level cosine similarity to NSD captions/images) are largely inherited from prior work (Singh et al., 2023) and are somewhat indirect proxies for 'true' voxel selectivity; there is no direct human behavioral validation or expert neuroscientist rating of caption quality/faithfulness.

The comparison between LaVCa and simple concatenation (Concat-N) in Figure 2 shows Concat-N actually achieves higher or comparable raw accuracy at larger N, and the paper's main selling point (conciseness/interpretability) is not quantitatively validated via, e.g., human readability/interpretability ratings—it's asserted qualitatively.

The 'lexical and semantic diversity' metrics (vocabulary size, PCA components, embedding variance) are relatively crude/superficial ways to demonstrate 'richness'; a larger vocabulary or higher variance does not necessarily mean captions are more accurate or meaningful (some example captions in the appendix, e.g., 'Eachkristilythemed mug...' or 'Woodnut coloured blue eyes', appear to contain nonsensical/garbled text, raising concerns about caption quality/coherence not captured by the chosen metrics).

Face-selective regions show notably weaker performance than other ROIs, and the paper's proposed explanation (loss of local features like eyes/nose during MLLM captioning) is speculative and untested by additional experiments.

The pipeline relies on a chain of black-box models (MiniCPM-V, gpt-4o, CLIP, MeaCap's Sentence Composer, FLUX.1) that individually introduces various forms of bias/noise, and it's unclear how much of the observed 'voxel selectivity' signal reflects genuine brain representations versus artifacts/priors of these pretrained models (e.g., dataset biases in OpenImages, language priors of gpt-4o).

No direct statistical comparison or discussion of computational cost/scalability versus BrainSCUBA (e.g., API costs of gpt-4o for tens of thousands of voxels), which affects reproducibility and practical adoption.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to BrainSCUBA and SASC—conceptually it combines ideas from both (image-based optimal stimuli selection akin to BrainSCUBA's approach, and LLM-based keyword summarization akin to SASC) rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (voxel-level interpretability of DNN-based encoding models) and proposes a modular pipeline that decouples optimal-image discovery from caption generation, allowing flexible use of different vision/LLM backbones.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: both sentence-level and image-level brain activity prediction are used, with shuffled controls, multiple top-N voxel subsets, and results reported across four subjects.
Extensive ablation studies (number of optimal images, number of keywords, keyword-extraction model) help characterize the method's hyperparameter sensitivity and justify design choices.

The ROI-level and UMAP-based qualitative analyses (e.g., within OFA/PPA) provide an interesting, fine-grained look at functional heterogeneity within canonically defined visual areas, which is a potentially useful contribution to visual neuroscience.
The paper is transparent about limitations (e.g., face-area underperformance, reliance on language limiting access to local visual features) and discusses plausible future extensions.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the method largely stitches together existing off-the-shelf components (CLIP encoding model, MiniCPM-V captioning, GPT-4o keyword extraction via an existing in-context-learning prompt template, and MeaCap's pre-existing Sentence Composer), with relatively little new methodological insight beyond this recombination.

The main baseline, BrainSCUBA, is not run with the original codebase/checkpoints (which are unavailable) but is reimplemented in-house with a different training procedure, different image dataset composition, and different encoding-model optimization (ridge regression vs. gradient descent). This introduces a confound: performance gaps could partly reflect reimplementation/optimization differences rather than the proposed method's genuine superiority, and the paper does not sufficiently stress-test or validate the reimplementation’s fidelity against reported BrainSCUBA numbers from the original paper.

The core evaluation metric (cosine/Sentence-BERT similarity between generated captions/images and NSD captions/images, correlated with measured activity) is an indirect proxy that is likely biased toward longer, more detailed, or more diverse captions — exactly the property that distinguishes LaVCa from BrainSCUBA. This raises concern that part of the reported gains reflect an evaluation-metric artifact (more words/concepts increasing embedding overlap with some image caption) rather than more accurate voxel-selectivity characterization; the paper's own Figure 2 analysis suggests word count strongly affects accuracy, undermining confidence that the sentence/image metrics isolate true explanatory quality.

Qualitative examples (e.g., "Eachkristilythemed mug features...", "This innovative sidewalk entrance overlaps with a train track...") reveal that many LaVCa captions are grammatically broken, incoherent, or semantically implausible given the underlying images, which undercuts the claimed gain in interpretability — a central selling point of the paper beyond prediction accuracy.

The study is restricted to a single fMRI dataset (NSD), four subjects, and one vision backbone (CLIP ViT-B/32); generality of the approach to other datasets/species/encoding model architectures is unestablished.

Statistical testing (paired t-test across voxels, FDR correction via permutation against independent Gaussian noise) does not clearly account for spatial autocorrelation among cortical voxels, which can inflate apparent significance.

The ROI 'fine-grained functional differentiation' and 'multi-concept voxel' claims are interesting but are supported mainly by qualitative inspection of a handful of hand-picked examples and word clouds, rather than a rigorous quantitative characterization of how many voxels truly exhibit such properties or how robust these patterns are across image-generation/caption-generation stochasticity.
No human evaluation of caption quality/faithfulness is conducted, despite the central claim being about generating interpretable, accurate natural-language descriptions for human consumption.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and important problem: voxel-level interpretability of DNN-based fMRI encoding models, moving beyond coarse group-level or end-to-end caption generation approaches like BrainSCUBA.

The proposed pipeline (encoding model -> optimal image retrieval -> MLLM captioning -> LLM keyword extraction and filtering -> sentence composition) is a sensible and modular decomposition that allows flexible substitution of vision/language components, in contrast to the end-to-end BrainSCUBA architecture.

Extensive quantitative evaluation across four NSD subjects, multiple voxel subsets (top-1000/3000/5000/10000), and two complementary metrics (sentence-level and image-level brain activity prediction), consistently showing improvements over BrainSCUBA and a shuffled control.

Thoughtful evaluation of interpretability-accuracy tradeoffs (LaVCa vs. Concat-N), demonstrating that the summarization step retains prediction accuracy while dramatically reducing caption length, which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Interesting downstream neuroscientific findings, such as fine-grained functional differentiation within ROIs (e.g., OFA, PPA) and evidence of multi-concept encoding within single voxels, which could be of interest to the cognitive neuroscience community.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (number of optimal images, number of keywords, keyword extraction model) and appendix analyses (BrainSCUBA temperature sweep, per-subject flatmaps) that support robustness of the main claims.
Good documentation of implementation details and prompts (in the appendix), which aids reproducibility despite reliance on proprietary models.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a recombination of existing off-the-shelf components (CLIP encoding models, MiniCPM-V captioning, GPT-4o keyword extraction, MeaCap's Sentence Composer) rather than a novel algorithmic or modeling advance; novelty is primarily in the pipeline design and application to voxel captioning.

BrainSCUBA baseline is a self-implemented reproduction (code not publicly released by original authors), and several implementation choices (dataset composition, encoding model training procedure) differ from the original paper, which introduces some uncertainty about whether the comparison is fully fair, despite the authors' efforts to control for dataset differences.

The method relies on proprietary, closed-source models (gpt-4o, MiniCPM-V) for core pipeline stages, which limits exact reproducibility and long-term stability of results as these APIs change or are deprecated.

Evaluation metrics (sentence-level and image-level similarity-based prediction) are somewhat indirect proxies for "caption quality" or "true voxel selectivity," and no human evaluation or expert neuroscientist judgment of caption plausibility/accuracy is reported.

Absolute prediction accuracies remain modest (e.g., ρ ~0.2-0.3), and the gap between LaVCa and BrainSCUBA, while statistically significant, is relatively small in absolute magnitude (e.g., 0.039 sentence-level improvement on subj01), raising questions about the practical/scientific significance of the improvement.

The qualitative UMAP/cluster analyses and example captions (Figures 5, A7-A15) are illustrative but somewhat subjective and cherry-picked (top-2 accuracy captions per cluster), making it hard to assess how representative or generalizable the highlighted findings on functional differentiation truly are.

Some generated captions in the appendix examples appear syntactically awkward or semantically incoherent (e.g., 'Woodnut coloured blue eyes...', run-on/garbled sentences), suggesting the Sentence Composer step sometimes produces lower-quality outputs that could undermine claims of high interpretability.

Limited discussion of computational cost/scalability of the four-stage pipeline (MLLM captioning + LLM extraction per voxel across many voxels and subjects), which could be a practical barrier to adoption.

strengths: Addresses an important and clearly motivated problem: interpreting voxel-level selectivity in DNN-based fMRI encoding models, which are otherwise black-box.

The proposed pipeline decouples optimal-image discovery from caption generation and uses LLM-based multi-keyword extraction plus a sentence composer, making the method modular and backbone-agnostic (any contrastive VLM, MLLM, or LLM can be swapped in), unlike prior end-to-end methods (BrainSCUBA, SASC).

Extensive and carefully designed evaluation: sentence-level and independent image-level (via generated images) prediction accuracy, permutation testing with FDR correction, shuffled-caption controls, and comparisons across multiple voxel-count thresholds (top-1000 to top-10000).

Thorough ablation studies in the appendix covering encoding model design (ridge vs. gradient descent, linear vs. nonlinear, voxel-wise vs. shared weights), VLM/MLLM/LLM choices, number of optimal images, number of keywords, prompting strategy, and the effect of the Sentence Composer — this level of rigor is uncommon and strengthens confidence in the design choices.
Demonstrates generalization to a second, independently collected fMRI dataset (BOLD5000) with consistent cross-dataset semantic patterns (word clouds), supporting robustness beyond NSD.

Provides a genuinely interesting neuroscientific finding: using quantitative clustering of captions, the paper shows that classically "category-selective" ROIs (OFA, PPA) encode a broader, multi-concept semantic space than traditionally assumed, with reproducibility across subjects.
Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, compute resource reporting, and an honest re-implementation of BrainSCUBA for fairer, dataset-controlled comparison.
weaknesses: The core evaluation metric (cosine similarity between caption/image embeddings and stimulus embeddings, correlated with brain activity) is an indirect proxy; absolute prediction accuracies remain modest (Spearman ρ ~0.2–0.3), so it is unclear how much of true voxel selectivity is actually captured versus superficial embedding overlap.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental relative to BrainSCUBA/SASC — the main contribution is decomposing the pipeline and using multi-keyword LLM summarization, rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea; gains over BrainSCUBA, while statistically significant, are numerically modest in several settings.

BrainSCUBA baseline is a self-reimplementation (original code unavailable at project start) with differing training data/procedure from the original paper, which raises some concern about comparison fairness despite the authors' efforts to control for dataset.

Face-selective regions (e.g., OFA/FFA) show comparatively weaker prediction performance, a limitation acknowledged by the authors but not resolved, weakening the generality of the central claims across all visual cortex regions.

Pipeline is computationally heavy (multiple large models: MLLM captioner, GPT-4o keyword extractor, CLIP encoders, text-to-image model for evaluation) and reportedly requires ~83 GPU-hours per subject for 20,000 voxels, raising scalability concerns for broader adoption.

No human evaluation of caption faithfulness/quality is conducted; all assessments rely on automated embedding-based metrics, which may not fully validate whether captions are semantically meaningful or accurate to human judgment.
BOLD5000 generalization results show a considerable accuracy drop and are validated mostly qualitatively (word clouds) rather than with the same statistical rigor as the primary NSD analyses.

Analysis is restricted to only 4 subjects (NSD) / 4 subjects (BOLD5000), consistent with the field but still limiting generalizability claims about universal representational richness in category-selective cortex.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: interpreting voxel-level selectivity from DNN-based encoding models via natural language captions, extending prior work (BrainSCUBA, SASC).

The pipeline is decomposed into clearly interpretable stages (encoding model, optimal image retrieval, MLLM captioning, keyword extraction/filtering, sentence composition), which is a sensible design that decouples image selection from caption generation and allows flexible substitution of VLM/LLM backbones.

Extensive empirical validation: results are reported across 4 NSD subjects, replicate on an independent dataset (BOLD5000), and include substantial ablations (encoding model architecture, VLM choice, number of optimal images/keywords, MLLM choice, prompting strategy, sentence-similarity model) in the appendix.

Quantitative evaluation uses both sentence-level and image-level metrics, with proper statistical testing (permutation test + FDR correction) and comparisons to a shuffled control and to a re-implemented BrainSCUBA baseline, as well as ablated single-keyword variants.

The lexical/semantic diversity analysis (inter- and intra-voxel) and ROI-level shuffling/quantitative analyses provide converging evidence that captions capture more than the coarse category labels traditionally used to describe regions like OFA/PPA, which is a potentially interesting neuroscientific finding.
Reasonable transparency about limitations (e.g., weaker performance in face-selective regions, inability to capture multimodal/cognitive voxels) and compute/resource reporting.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core pipeline largely stitches together existing off-the-shelf components (MiniCPM-V for captioning, GPT-4o for keyword extraction, the MeaCap Sentence Composer for sentence generation, CLIP for encoding/filtering) rather than proposing new modeling or algorithmic advances; the contribution is primarily an engineering/pipeline combination.

The quantitative evaluation metrics (Sentence-BERT cosine similarity to NSD captions as a proxy for predicted activity, and CLIP-embedding similarity between generated images and stimuli) are indirect proxies whose validity as ground truth for voxel semantics is not independently validated (e.g., no human judgment/interpretability study of whether captions are actually faithful or meaningful to human raters).

Reported prediction accuracies (Spearman's rho typically ~0.15-0.3) are modest in absolute terms; while statistically significant and better than baselines, the practical/interpretive significance of such correlations for claiming richer semantic understanding is not strongly established.

The comparison to BrainSCUBA relies on the authors' own re-implementation (since original code was unavailable), raising some concern about the fairness/faithfulness of this baseline, despite efforts described in the appendix to match training data and hyperparameters.

Heavy reliance on closed, non-reproducible components (GPT-4o via OpenAI API) for a core step (keyword extraction) limits exact reproducibility and could introduce version-dependent variability over time.

The paper's main claims about richer representational content in classically category-selective ROIs (e.g., OFA, PPA) could partly reflect noise, encoding-model imperfections, or LLM/keyword-extraction artifacts rather than genuine neural multi-concept selectivity; the paper does not fully rule out such alternative explanations despite some control analyses (e.g., shuffled captions).

Much of the substantive analysis and validation is relegated to a very large appendix (50 pages total), making the main paper comparatively thin on quantitative depth and potentially harder to assess without reading the appendix in full.

The face-selective region limitation (OFA/FFA underperforming) is acknowledged but not resolved, suggesting the captioning approach may systematically miss fine-grained local features important for some ROI types, weakening the generality of the richer-than-assumed claim across all cortex.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem (voxel-level interpretability of DNN-based encoding models) with a clean four-stage pipeline that decouples optimal-image selection, image captioning, and keyword-based sentence composition, making the method modular and applicable to any VLM/LLM backbone.

Extensive quantitative evaluation: sentence-level and image-level brain-activity prediction accuracy across four NSD subjects and multiple top-N voxel subsets, with permutation testing and FDR correction for statistical rigor, plus a shuffled-caption control that serves as a meaningful sanity check.

Thorough ablation studies in the appendix covering VLM backbone choice, number of optimal images, number of keywords, MLLM/LLM choice, prompting strategy, sentence-composer effect, and sentence-similarity model choice, which substantially strengthens confidence in the design choices.

Generalization test on an independent dataset (BOLD5000) with different subjects/scanner parameters, showing consistent ROI-level semantic patterns, which supports robustness of the findings beyond NSD.

Rich qualitative analyses (word clouds, UMAP projections, cross-subject cluster reproducibility) that provide neuroscientifically interesting evidence of within-ROI semantic diversity beyond classical single-category selectivity accounts (e.g., faces in OFA, places in PPA).

Careful comparison methodology against BrainSCUBA (including a fair in-house reimplementation using the same image pool) and lexical/semantic diversity metrics that control for caption length, mitigating trivial explanations for improved performance.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental — the pipeline largely recombines existing components (contrastive VLM encoding models, MLLM captioning, LLM keyword extraction, and MeaCap's sentence composer) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the closest prior works (BrainSCUBA, SASC) already establish the data-driven captioning paradigm.

The primary evaluation metric (Sentence-BERT/CLIP-text similarity-based prediction accuracy) is an indirect proxy for caption faithfulness/interpretability rather than a direct or human-judged measure of whether captions actually describe voxel selectivity meaningfully; no human evaluation of caption quality or faithfulness is reported.

Heavy dependence on a closed-source, potentially non-reproducible component (GPT-4o via API) for keyword extraction undermines long-term reproducibility, since API model versions can change or be deprecated; the reproducibility statement also leaves the code repository link blank/unspecified in the visible text.

Practical scalability is limited: the reported ~83 GPU-hours per subject for 20,000 voxels raises concerns about applicability to larger-scale or whole-brain analyses, or to labs without significant compute resources.

Face-selective ROIs (e.g., OFA, FFA) show comparatively lower prediction accuracy, and the paper's own limitation discussion suggests the MLLM captioning step may miss fine-grained local features (eyes, nose) — a real gap not fully resolved by the proposed pipeline.

Diversity/interpretability claims (vocabulary size, PCA dimensionality, UMAP cluster spread) are somewhat correlational and could partly reflect the richer vocabulary of GPT-4o/keyword extraction rather than a deeper or more accurate characterization of the voxel's true representational content; distinguishing genuine semantic richness from mere lexical variety remains only partially addressed.
